summary: Defines RADIUS, a protocol carrying authentication, authorization, and configuration information between a network access server and a shared authentication server. It was replaced by RFC 2138.

eli5.summary: When you dial in, the front desk calls a central office to check you are allowed in. RADIUS is that call.

subtitle: Central authentication server for dial-in networks and access control.

tldr.problem: Dial-in services and wide-area networks needed a way to centrally authenticate users and deliver configuration to network access servers, rather than managing user databases on each server individually.
tldr.mechanism: RADIUS defines a client-server protocol where a Network Access Server (NAS) sends authentication requests to a central RADIUS server using UDP. The server authenticates the user and returns authorization details and configuration information.
tldr.outcome: RADIUS became widely deployed for dial-in authentication, but was obsoleted by RFC 2138 with improvements.

today: RADIUS was originally published as RFC 2058 but was obsoleted by RFC 2138 with clarifications and updates.

sections.title: The Problem and Client-Server Model
sections.content:
RADIUS is the Remote Authentication Dial In User Service. Managing a large number of dial-in users across multiple modems required maintaining user databases on each access server, which became administratively expensive and insecure. RADIUS solves this by centralizing the user database.

RADIUS uses a client-server model: the Network Access Server (NAS), such as a modem bank or dial-in concentrator, is the client. It sends authentication requests to a shared RADIUS server. The RADIUS server authenticates the user against a central database, consults authorization rules, and sends back configuration information the NAS needs to provide service to the user. The NAS acts on the response immediately.

A RADIUS server can also act as a proxy, forwarding requests to other authentication servers or other RADIUS servers.
sections.eli5: The modem pool (the client) phones the central database (the server) to ask "Is this person allowed in and what settings should I give them?" The server checks the database and phones back the answer.

sections.title: How Authentication Works
sections.content:
A RADIUS authentication conversation starts when the NAS client creates an Access-Request packet containing the user's credentials. The packet includes the user's name (User-Name) and password (encrypted using MD5), the NAS identifier, and the port the user is accessing. The NAS sends this to the RADIUS server on UDP port 1812.

The RADIUS server validates the client (checking that it has a shared secret with the NAS), then verifies the user's credentials against its database. The server responds with one of three packets: Access-Accept (success), Access-Reject (failure), or Access-Challenge (for multifactor authentication or challenge-response systems).

If the server sends Access-Challenge, the NAS displays the challenge to the user (for example, a number from a security token), the user responds, and the NAS sends a new Access-Request with the response. This cycle can repeat until the server sends Accept or Reject.
sections.eli5: The modem sends "User Alice, password [secret code]" to the RADIUS server. The server looks up Alice, checks her password, and sends back "yes" or "no." For some users, the server can ask a follow-up question first.

sections.title: Packets and Security
sections.content:
RADIUS packets are sent over UDP, a simple connectionless protocol. Each packet contains a Code field (1 octet) that identifies its type, an Identifier to match requests and replies, a Length field, a 16-octet Authenticator (which is different for requests vs. responses), and Attributes.

Security relies on a shared secret between the NAS and RADIUS server. For requests, the Authenticator is a 16-octet random number. For responses, the Authenticator is an MD5 hash of the response packet concatenated with the shared secret. User passwords are hidden by XORing them with an MD5 hash of the shared secret and Request Authenticator, preventing them from being sent in clear text.

The minimum packet size is 20 octets; the maximum is 4096. The minimum payload is 576 octets, enough for authentication systems of the time.
sections.eli5: The packets are tiny envelopes with a secret code on them, so both sides can verify they are talking to each other and not an impostor. The password is scrambled so no one listening in can steal it.

sections.title: Packet Types and Their Meanings
sections.content:
RADIUS defines several packet types by their Code value. Access-Request (Code 1) is sent by the NAS with user credentials. Access-Accept (Code 2) is the server's positive response, containing service configuration attributes. Access-Reject (Code 3) denies the user and may include a text message. Access-Challenge (Code 11) is sent by the server when it wants to challenge the user with a multi-factor scheme.

Each reply packet includes the Identifier from the request, allowing the NAS to match the response to the original request. This is important because the NAS may send multiple overlapping requests to the same or different servers.
sections.eli5: Different packet types mean "Please check this user," "User is okay," "User is not okay," or "Ask the user another question." The NAS knows which answer goes with which request by the packet ID, like a return address on a letter.

sections.title: Attributes: Configuration and Authorization
sections.content:
RADIUS Attributes are variable-length Type-Length-Value tuples that carry the actual authentication, authorization, and configuration details. The Type field (1 octet) identifies the attribute type; Length is the total size of the attribute; Value contains the data.

Common attributes include User-Name (who is logging in), User-Password (encrypted), Service-Type (what kind of service: login, PPP, telnet, etc.), Framed-Protocol (PPP or SLIP), Framed-IP-Address (the IP address to assign), Framed-IP-Netmask, MTU size, routing information, and compression settings. Vendor-Specific attributes (Type 26) allow vendors to extend RADIUS with proprietary configuration options.

The RFC specifies over 40 standard attributes. The protocol is extensible: implementations can ignore unknown attribute types, allowing new attributes to be added without breaking existing servers and clients.
sections.eli5: Attributes are little labels inside the packet that say things like "User Alice," "IP address 192.168.1.5," or "This is a PPP connection." New labels can be invented and old systems just skip them if they do not understand.

sections.title: Why UDP and Not TCP?
sections.content:
RADIUS uses UDP instead of TCP for several reasons. First, RADIUS is a stateless, transaction-based protocol. Clients and servers can reboot independently without special handling. UDP eliminates the need for TCP's connection management overhead. Second, RADIUS has different timing requirements than TCP: the user is willing to wait several seconds for authentication, but not minutes. If the primary RADIUS server is slow or down, the client can quickly retry with an alternate server without waiting for TCP timeouts. Third, UDP simplifies server implementation; early RADIUS servers were multithreaded and spawned separate processes to handle each request, responding directly to the client's UDP port.

The tradeoff is that RADIUS implementations must manage retransmission timers themselves, but this is simpler than TCP's aggressive retransmission and acknowledgement overhead for this particular use case.
sections.eli5: UDP is like tossing messages across the room: fast and simple. TCP is like a phone call: reliable but more complex. For asking "Is this user allowed?" the fast way is better.
